item.title: Amakusa Islands — Guide
item.description: The Amakusa Islands, a beautiful chain of over a hundred islands off the west coast of Kumamoto, combine gorgeous coastal scenery with fascinating history and abundant wildlife. Connected to the mainland and each other by a series of bridges (the ‘Amakusa Five Bridges’) and ferries, they are one of the best places in Japan for wild dolphin watching, with resident pods of bottlenose dolphins seen year-round on boat tours. Amakusa also has a poignant Christian history: it was a stronghold of persecuted ‘hidden Christians’ and the centre of the 1637 Shimabara-Amakusa Rebellion, and its churches and related sites form part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing.

item.title: Diving & Snorkelling in Kagoshima's Islands — Guide
item.description: The warm, clear seas around Kagoshima’s southern islands — especially Yakushima, Amami Oshima and the Amami archipelago — make the prefecture one of Japan’s finest destinations for diving and snorkelling. Bathed by the warm Kuroshio current, these waters teem with life: vibrant coral reefs, schools of tropical fish, sea turtles, rays and, in places, larger marine life, all in visibility that can be superb. Around Yakushima, divers explore reefs and granite underwater landscapes and often encounter sea turtles, while Amami’s extensive coral reefs and lagoons are a highlight of southern Japanese diving.

item.title: Nagasaki's Outer Islands Day Trip — Guide
item.description: Nagasaki prefecture includes a great many islands scattered across the seas off its long, deeply indented coast, and a day trip out to them offers a relaxed, scenic contrast to the historic city. Reached by ferry or high-speed boat from Nagasaki and other ports, the outlying islands offer clear blue seas, white-sand beaches, rugged coastal scenery, quiet fishing villages and a slower pace of island life. Depending on the island, visitors can swim and snorkel in summer, sample the freshest local seafood, walk coastal paths and viewpoints, and soak up the peaceful, remote atmosphere far from the crowds.

item.title: Sea Kayaking in the Seto Inland Sea — Guide
item.description: The Seto Inland Sea off Imabari, with its calm sheltered waters, gentle tides and countless small islands, is one of the loveliest places in Japan for sea kayaking. Guided kayak tours let you paddle out among the islands of the Shimanami Kaido area, gliding across clear blue water, exploring hidden coves and pebble beaches, and passing beneath the soaring spans of the great suspension bridges from water level — a completely different perspective on the famous cycling route.

item.title: Seto Inland Sea Island Cruise: Sailing Between the Islands — Guide
item.description: The Seto Inland Sea, the sheltered water between Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu, is one of Japan’s most beautiful landscapes and was its first designated national park. Strewn with hundreds of green, steeply rising islands and famously calm, it has been a highway for a thousand years, and the best way to appreciate it is simply to get on a boat. Options range from local ferries linking island ports for a few hundred yen, to sightseeing cruises from Hiroshima and Onomichi, to overnight luxury cruise ships.

item.title: Setouchi Triennale: Art Island Hopping — Guide
item.description: The Setouchi Triennale is a celebrated contemporary art festival held once every three years across around a dozen islands and ports of the Seto Inland Sea, with Kagawa’s Takamatsu as a main gateway. Spread over three seasonal sessions (spring, summer, autumn), it fills the islands — Naoshima, Teshima, Shodoshima, Ogijima, Megijima and more — with hundreds of artworks, installations and events, many set in old houses, terraced fields, harbours and disused buildings, deeply connected to island life and landscape.

item.title: Shimanami Kaido Cycling: Island-Hopping by Bike — Guide
item.description: The Shimanami Kaido is the finest cycling route in Japan and one of the best anywhere: a roughly 70-kilometre course running from Onomichi in Hiroshima across six islands of the Seto Inland Sea to Imabari in Shikoku. Uniquely, every bridge on the route carries a dedicated, separated cycle lane with gentle spiral approach ramps, so riders cross high above the sea in complete safety. Between the bridges the route rolls through fishing villages, citrus groves and quiet island roads, with a blue line painted on the tarmac guiding you the whole way.

item.title: Shimanami Kaido: The Island Cycling Route — Guide
item.description: The Shimanami Kaido is one of the world’s great cycling routes, a roughly 70-kilometre expressway that leaps across six islands of the Seto Inland Sea on a series of magnificent bridges, linking Imabari in Ehime with Onomichi in Hiroshima. Uniquely, it has a dedicated cycling and pedestrian path running its entire length, letting you ride high over sparkling blue straits, past islands dotted with orchards, shrines and beaches. You can cycle the whole route in a day, take it slowly over two with island stops, or just ride a scenic section — rental bikes and drop-off points make it easy for all levels.

item.title: The Seto Inland Sea Island Landscape — Guide
item.description: The Seto Inland Sea (Setouchi) is one of Japan’s most beloved landscapes, a vast, calm, sheltered sea enclosed by Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu and studded with hundreds of green islands large and small. Long a highway of trade and culture, its serene beauty — gentle water, layered island silhouettes, fishing boats and famous sunsets — has inspired poets, artists and travellers for centuries. Kagawa sits right on its shore, and the seascape shapes everything: the ferries fanning out to the islands, the great bridges (like the Seto Ohashi) leaping across it, the island communities and the art destinations of Naoshima and beyond.

item.title: Shimanami Kaido: The Complete Cycling Guide from Imabari to Onomichi
item.description: The Shimanami Kaido connects Imabari in Ehime to Onomichi in Hiroshima Prefecture across 70 kilometres of bridges and islands spanning the Seto Inland Sea. It is widely regarded as the world’s most scenic cycling route, and it earns that description not through superlative natural spectacle but through something quieter: a sustained sense of moving through island light over calm blue-grey water, with small fishing ports and citrus-scented hillsides at every stop.
